steps.say: This lesson shows the loop at the heart of os-shell, the one program that draws everything a person sees. Each turn of the loop is a **frame**: read input, decide what to show, draw it, put it on the screen, then sleep until something happens.
At start it opens the framebuffer, the screen's memory that it draws into, and the keyboard and pointer.
It is also a Wayland compositor, the program Linux apps send their windows to. That is how Firefox or Prism appear inside the person's design.
If a mind is set up, the saved design comes back from /etc/os/facet.xml. That is the desktop document of lesson 07.

steps.through: if (A.now < paced_until) { /* between two frames: only the apps answered */
steps.say: A frame is drawn at most every 16 ms, about 60 a second. Between frames only the apps' messages are answered.
Input is read into `A.in` once per frame. `A` holds the whole desktop's state, and `PROF` times each step for the performance log.
`frame_wanted` decides whether anything may have changed. If not, nothing is drawn, apart from one frame every 250 ms for clocks and blinking cursors.

steps.say: These are the reasons it may draw. Every 30 seconds the log says which ones kept it busy, in a line starting `frames:`.

steps.anchor: if (lock_frame()) /* locked: the lock screen is everything (lock.c) */
steps.through: if (family_frame()) /* a child's computer, time's up (or outside the hours set): that is everything */
steps.say: The lock screen comes first, then the child lock's "time's up". Either can take the whole frame.
Otherwise one screen is drawn: the first-boot screens, onboarding, the designing screen, or the desktop itself.
Drawing happens in memory, in software. **Presenting** copies the finished picture to the screen in one go, so nothing half-drawn is seen.
Then it sleeps in `poll` until a key, the pointer, an app or a timer wakes it. Sleeping is what keeps an idle desktop from using the processor.
`desktop_draw` is the desktop's own part of the frame: the preview, the companion, the agent, voice, then the design's layout and the windows, in order.
Next: **07 Facet, the design language**, which is what desktop_draw lays out and draws.
